item.title: Journalists across Asia face police action in growing crackdown on movements. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“I was put in a bus. I showed them that I have an ID card and a mic ID, and asked them why I was being detained. But they didn’t want us to show how protesters were being manhandled,” said 28-year-old Pragya Mishra, who runs a news outlet called Ulta Chasma uc.
On October 11, 2026, Mishra was covering the protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at RK Ashram in Delhi. While reporting, Mishra says her cameraperson Anuj Kumar (23) was pulled by his hair by police personnel. When she went to protect him and inform the police that they were from the media, she was also forcibly put inside a bus with a few other journalists.
She told Asian Dispatch that she was being taken to a detention centre in Rajendra Nagar. The bus, however, was intercepted and stopped by other journalists. She says that the police eventually dropped them at Connaught Place.
Mishra was not the only journalist who faced police action during the recent protests held across the country against Kumar over the alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.
The protest against CEC Kumar is linked to the alleged irregularities in the ongoing SIR process, which has reportedly resulted in the deletion of around 13 crore names from electoral rolls.
It gained momentum after a report published by The Indian Express dated September 24 found that Election Commissioners Sukhir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period.
According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), at least 43 instances of journalists being detained were recorded. Journalists from several news organizations such as The Wire, Scroll, The Quint, Newslaundry, as well as freelance journalists were detained -- some were even heckled, assaulted, and forced to delete what they had documented on the ground.
The Press Club of India, along with other journalists’ associations, condemned the detentions and said that the police took the step even after journalists displayed their press cards.
It further mentioned that the police seized the phones and reporting equipment of some of the journalists. The statement referred to the developments as a “blatant attack on the freedom of the press.”
Commenting on the situation, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) told us: “What we are witnessing is not simply excessive policing during demonstrations, it is part of a broader pattern of restrictions that undermines the ability of journalists to report freely on matters of public interest, particularly when their reporting exposes the conduct of the authorities.”
RSF is an international non-profit working towards protecting the rights of journalists/press. According to their 2026 World Press Freedom Index , India ranks 157 out of 180 countries in press freedom. The body also highlighted that press freedom remains a major concern across Asia, where the media faces restrictions in covering politically sensitive events and protests.
CPJ’s annual report on jailed journalists, released in January 2026, noted that 330 journalists were behind the bars globally as of December 1, 2025. Of these, one-third were in Asia -- China and Myanmar were found to be the leading jailers in the region.
It’s important to note that this number from Asia excludes jailed journalists from Central and West Asia (referred to as the Middle East in the graph). Those are marked separately in CPJ’s database.
Speaking to Asian Dispatch , Kunal Majumder, Asia-Pacific program coordinator, Committee to Project Journalists (CPJ), said that journalism is under attack across the region and added: “In South Asia, the focus is largely on over-regulation of the online space; apart from SLAPP [Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation] suits, physical violence remains a grave problem.”
Expressing concern about the situation in India, Majumder said that India has a responsibility to uphold press freedom and “serve as a role model for other countries in the Global South.”
This pattern where journalists have faced action, have been assaulted, detained or arrested by law enforcement agencies is consistent across other Asian countries.
For instance: the situation for journalists in Bangladesh during the 2024 July uprising was alarming. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) estimated that at least 160 journalists were reportedly injured while covering the nationwide protests as of July 31, 2024.
RSF noted that five journalists were allegedly killed by police bullets between July 15, 2024 and August 5, 2024, and one was killed during clashes between two factions.
CPJ, in a report published on July 26, 2024, detailed the reports of police attacks on journalists. It said that on July 16, 2024, police personnel fired metal pellets at journalists Mehedi Mamun, Abdur Rahman Khan Sarjil, Wajahatul Islam, and Jubayer Ahmed. This happened despite them identifying themselves as journalists.
The next day, July 17, 2024, Abdullah Al Mamum, a correspondent with Prothom Alo, was reportedly beaten with rifles and batons by police personnel while he was recording the police action against students. Mamum told CPJ that he showed them his press card but he was beaten and the police fired a rubber bullet at him while he was trying to flee.
More recently, Ernest Cruz, a reporter working with Bulatlat in the Philippines, was assaulted by the Quezon City Police on October 19, 2026, while he was covering a protest led by farmer groups. According to RSF, Cruz was assaulted despite identifying himself as a journalist.
A similar incident happened on September 21, 2025, when eight journalists covering the anti-government protests in Manila were harassed, assaulted, and obstructed. They alleged that police used shields to deliberately obstruct media coverage. The usage of tear gas and water cannons near to where journalists were also posed direct harm to their safety.
At least nine journalists in Sri Lanka were injured during the anti-government protests in 2022. A freelance journalist, Sumedha Sanjeewa Gallage, was reportedly attacked by the police while he was covering a demonstration outside the president’s residence. As per reports , he lost partial vision in his right eye following the attack.
The 2026 CPJ analysis also found that the greatest incidence of torture and beatings of journalists has occurred in Iran since 1992. Between 2022 and 2025, 71 journalists were imprisoned in Iran.
Mishra, who was bundled in a bus in New Delhi on October 11, highlighted that these detentions happened despite the Supreme Court clearly stating that lawyers and journalists should be allowed to work without hindrance.
“The Supreme Court had ordered that journalists, lawyers, and doctors should be allowed to continue their work…I pointed this out, but they [police] weren’t listening,” Mishra says. She also told us that she repeatedly asked the police personnel not to carry her and that she could walk to the bus, but nobody heard her.
Speaking about the detentions and the force with which journalists were met, RSF said, “The circumstances strongly suggest that journalists were targeted precisely because they were documenting what was happening on the ground: the police's brutal treatment of protesters. Several journalists were detained while filming arrests or acts of police violence. Others had their phones seized, their cameras damaged or were pressured to delete their footage. This raises serious concerns that the objective was to prevent images of police operations from reaching the public.”
Several journalists, who were covering the protests, also highlighted on social media that the police was asking for government accredited press cards and not recognising cards issued by independent organizations.
“ This raises fundamental concerns, press freedom cannot be conditional on government approval, and accreditation requirements must never become a tool for excluding independent or critical voices. The right to report does not depend on whether a journalist works for an established newspaper, an independent online outlet or a digital platform. All journalists must receive equal protection, regardless of their employer and professional status,” RSF said.
In Bangladesh, IFJ documented an expansion of gatekeeping intended to restrict the media’s ability to report. The Press Information Department had revoked the accreditation of around 167 journalists between October 29, 2024 and November 7, 2024.
These measures often lead to self-censorship .
The United Nations’ Human Rights Committee, in 2020 , adopted general comment number 37 that noted that the right to peaceful assembly should be recognized. It also highlighted the obligations of state parties regarding the same.
It said that law enforcement officials must respect and ensure the exercise of fundamental rights of organisers and participants, while also protecting journalists, observers, and others from harm.
The committee further said, “The role of journalists, human rights defenders, election monitors and others involved in monitoring or reporting on assemblies is of particular importance for the full enjoyment of the right of peaceful assembly.” It added that journalists and participants have the right to record law enforcement officials.
Majumder emphasised that every journalist has an equal right to report on public events without intimidation, obstruction, or discrimination. “The police must not decide who gets to do their job based on which media organisation they represent or what their reporting might reveal. Press freedom means protecting the right of all journalists to report, including those whose coverage may be critical of the authorities,” he said.
With respect to what happened in India, RSF recommended that courts should provide effective and timely remedies when journalists’ rights are violated, and newsrooms should strengthen safety protocols. It also said that the police must put an end to physical assaults, intimidation and the confiscation of journalistic equipment.
“Let us do our jobs. We don’t want any special or VIP treatment. We already go through a lot when we are on the ground…If the fourth pillar of democracy, which is journalism, is weakened, then what will happen to democracy?” said Mishra.
Abhishek is the associate editor at Asian Dispatch. Previously, he worked as the senior correspondent, fact-check for The Quint. The story was originally published by Asian Dispatch on October 22, 2026, and has been republished by Dhaka Tribune with permission.

item.title: Borrowing for our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The World Bank’s support to improve the quality of primary education and address learning gaps among children in Bangladesh is certainly positive news.
Aimed at improving learning outcomes, upgrading classrooms, providing essential learning materials, and strengthening school management for over 26 million children from pre-primary to Grade 5, we must be thankful that steps are being taken to improve the quality of a system where World Bank data show that around 50% of 10-year-old children in the country cannot read and understand a simple text appropriate for their age and grade level.
With that said, the approval of the $300 million financing package, while undeniably being a critical injection of resources into our foundational schooling system, must be recognized for what it is.
Every time international loans are secured for public development, a familiar shadow looms over the country: The deep-seated fear of administrative waste, corruption, bureaucratic leakage, and poor execution.
For decades, foreign-funded projects, regardless of the sector they are in, have too often been characterized by inflated costs and delayed rollouts that fail to bring about meaningful transformation.
Pouring hundreds of millions of dollars without ironclad execution safeguards is an unacceptable gamble. As such, the authorities concerned must recognize that this funding carries a heavy moral and economic obligation.
Every single taka must be channeled directly into measurable pedagogical improvements. There is no room for procurement corruption or administrative foot-dragging.
Foreign loans must build the nation’s future, not line the pockets of the influential and powerful, or disappear into bureaucratic black holes. If we are going to borrow to educate our children, we must ensure the investment delivers a measurable return -- transforming public primary education from a broken system into one that adds to our prosperity.

item.title: Holding the world accountable for the climate crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As world leaders assemble in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), it is safe to say that the threat of climate change has long ceased to be an abstract projection and has become the most significant existential catastrophe for the entire planet.
This is particularly true for a nation such as ours. With global heat records continuously shattered and fragile coastal ecosystems buckling under systemic salinization and relentless riverine erosion, Bangladesh remains among the most affected nations - due to a crisis it had virtually no part in creating.
For decades, global climate summits have yielded ambitious rhetoric, bureaucratic inertia, and pledges devoid of enforcement. At COP31, our diplomatic delegation, and indeed others from the Global South, must enter negotiations not to petition for international goodwill, but to demand the immediate, enforceable execution of climate justice.
The bedrock of our negotiating must reflect the economic reality we face as a result of climate change. Bangladeshi leadership must resolutely hold the world’s primary industrial polluters, ie the Global North accountable.
At a time when Bangladesh is experiencing among its most challenging economic issues, the effects of climate change continue to destroy infrastructure, deplete agricultural yields, and cause mass human displacement. Yet, it has been sad to see international countermeasures remain egregiously disproportionate.
The global Loss and Damage Fund, which was secured after years of arduous diplomacy, remains severely undercapitalized, with current allocation frameworks failing to address the true scope of vulnerability.
At COP31, Bangladesh must lead the coalition of climate-vulnerable states in advocating for legally binding financial commitments and doing away with the unreliable paradigm of voluntary contributions that major economies routinely disregard.
Beyond loss and damage, we must also prioritize direct, grant-based adaptation capital. Bangladesh cannot continue to accept climate finance structured as debt-bearing loans, which serve only to exacerbate existing foreign reserve strains.
Global climate equity is not optional, and COP31 must mark a turning point where Bangladesh plays its part in compelling the international community to honour its obligations.

item.title: The muddying of the waters. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir, when answering journalists’ questions on various serious subjects, often tries to create a little humor with some sarcasm and mockery.
Recently, Kabir was asked whether former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had applied for a passport to return to the country. The question can’t be called entirely reasonable, since there has been nothing to suggest that Hasina has applied for a passport at all.
In other words, the person about whom the passport question is being asked has herself said nothing about a passport. Anyway, if a journalist is curious, they will naturally ask, and a responsible official could be expected to give a proper answer.
The state minister said he knows nothing about a passport. Of course, he wouldn’t, because Sheikh Hasina has said nothing about a passport or a travel pass. Kabir, however, did not stop there.
“Is she going to come here to visit her in-laws’ home in Rangpur, that I should give her a passport, and she’ll come with the passport?” He described the matter as “laughable.” Then he laid out the government’s position in his own words.
“Sheikh Hasina is a fugitive terrorist. A dictator, a runaway terrorist,” he said.
Kabir’s choice of words here is quite interesting. Humayun Kabir is a Britain-based expatriate, so he knows well what “terrorist” means in the Western world. There, “terrorist” mainly means Islamist militants (although in the United States some armed white supremacist groups are designated as “domestic terrorist” organizations). Here a suspicion remains that, by labeling Hasina a “terrorist,” the minister wants to create an image of her in the minds of Westerners.
On bringing Hasina back from India, Kabir stood firm on his earlier position. “We have an active extradition treaty for catching terrorists, for catching criminals,” he said. “To catch terrorists and criminals, you don’t need a passport; they are handed over.”
He is right about this. The very purpose of the extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India is to arrest each other’s “terrorists” and “criminals” and send them back.
The problem lies elsewhere. Does India see Sheikh Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal” at all?
From the answer that Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi recently gave to a university student’s question at an event, no one should have any doubt that the Indian government, far from considering Sheikh Hasina a terrorist or criminal, treats her with considerable respect. Throughout his entire statement, Trivedi addressed the former PM as “Hasinaji.” Those with even the slightest idea of Indian social customs know that in that country, no responsible person adds “ ji ” to the name of a criminal or terrorist.
Is a passport a citizen’s right?
Trivedi had said that Hasina came to India on August 5, 2024 as the prime minister of Bangladesh. He also said the Indian Air Force did not “rescue” her from Ganabhaban. It was Bangladesh’s own military that took her to Delhi for her safety.
If India does not see Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal,” there is considerable room for doubt about whether the extradition treaty, however active, would apply in her case.
There is a second problem with Humayun Kabir’s statement. The government’s spokesperson and the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Policy and Strategy, Zahed Ur Rahman, said something slightly different a day earlier.
When he was asked multiple questions on the same subject at his regular press briefing, he did not directly rule out the possibility of giving Hasina a passport. He said he knows Hasina has made no such application, and that the government has no plan sitting ready.
“If it were the case that she (Hasina) had asked for it (a passport), then what the government would do, I think it is better to keep that to answer at that time.”
Rahman’s reply lightly touches on another aspect, whose importance is immense. He brought up the issue of citizenship, and he spoke of “this state,” that is, the state that was founded under the leadership of Hasina’s father.
Leaving the country and coming back is the constitutional right of all citizens of “this state” -- getting the document needed for travel, that is, a passport, is also their right. But under Bangladeshi law, in certain cases a citizen’s passport can be canceled, and they can be barred from leaving the country, and likewise an application for a passport can be rejected.
But canceling or rejecting a passport is all done to stop someone from leaving the country. The matter of returning to the country from abroad remains somewhat murky.
Extradition versus return
Hundreds of cases have been filed against Sheikh Hasina; one or two have been “tried” in her absence, and she has even been given the death sentence. The government considers Hasina a “fugitive,” so surely the government would want her to return and come under the country’s law?
Since Hasina has expressed a wish to return voluntarily in December, that apparently seems the easiest and quickest path. On the other hand, the extradition that Humayun Kabir speaks of, which Zahed Ur Rahman dramatically explains as “we will bring her by catching her,” is a long legal process; nobody can say how many months, or even years, the extradition process might take.
And even after the process ends, there is no guarantee that the Indian government will actually hand Sheikh Hasina over to face the death sentence.
Against this background, if the government chooses the long extradition process as the only road, and dismisses the possibility of a quick return with some absurd remark, then only one conclusion can be drawn: The government in fact does not want Sheikh Hasina to return to the country. That is, the government does not want the verdict in Hasina’s concluded trial to be carried out.
Listening to the state minister, it does not seem that Hasina’s presence in the country is desirable to the government. There could be two reasons.
First, in the current situation, the government has neither the political courage nor the strength to carry out the verdict against Sheikh Hasina.
Second, Hasina’s return would, on the one hand, revive the Awami League, and on the other, push the anger of Jamaat-e-Islami and the NCP to its peak. Perhaps the BNP lacks the confidence to face this two-sided political challenge.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: The future of biodiversity relies on shared consensus. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Governments, civil society, scientists, youth, academia, artists, and media professionals gathered under the theme of 'Taking Action for Nature' at COP17 Armenia to bring about collective action on biodiversity protection and nature restoration.
Reviewing targets and protocols
COP17 Armenia conducted the first global review of the collective implementation progress of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). The KMGBF is set on 23 global biodiversity targets which are to be completed by 2030 in line with the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS).
Targets two and three, restoring 30% of all degraded ecosystems and conserving and effectively managing 30% of land, waters, and seas, respectively, took precedence in the KMGBF discussions. There has also been significant discourse on how KMGBF can be financed, how actors and stakeholders responsible for it can be accountable, and how its credibility can be ensured.
Strengthening biosafety by monitoring living modified organisms (LMO), reduction of invasive alien species, compliance and accountability, monitoring and evaluation, and ensuring gender equality and gender-responsive approach for biodiversity action were also discussed.
There was little difference in technical opinion on biodiversity protection, but there is hesitation in resource mobilization and funding implementation.
These conversations generated three critical questions:
The commitment to address these grand questions is there, but the scale, strength, and pace of the decisions are not enough.
One reason is the slow implementation of the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAP) adopted by countries around the world. Another reason is the current economic and geopolitical trend. Their connection to biodiversity damage is not talked about enough.
The current global biodiversity funding gap stands at $700 billion. The GEF-9 Replenishment was announced, where new countries pledged close to $4.4bn. This barely scratches the surface of the gap. The CALI Fund adopted in COP16 Cali, Colombia garnered a lot of attention. It was initially created to collect private-sector contributions from industries that rely on genetic data in nature, for example big pharma, biotech companies, cosmetics giants, etc.
However, voluntary contributions have been measly. No major corporation contributed to the CALI Fund. Participants mainly talked about ensuring fair and equitable commercialisation and benefit-sharing of genetic data.
The polarity of financing perspectives is a recurring challenge that raises questions. Developing countries seek international finance to do the work. Developed countries, on the other hand, urged diversification of funding sources.
But how can we generate financial mechanisms that ensure direct access to local communities? How can we combine grants, loans, and other financial instruments to develop these mechanisms? How can we achieve more transparency in these processes?
The rights of nature and people
Target 18 of the KMGBF, which is reducing incentives and subsidies harmful for biodiversity by at least $500bn (for example phasing out pesticides) and introducing positive incentives without affecting biodiversity was up for debate and requires great political will.
This also applies to biodiversity-protected areas. There are calls to ensure improved and practical ecosystem development, biodiversity protection coordinated with livelihoods, community rights, and equitable governance.
One way is to acknowledge the legal rights of nature. Advocates explained how ecosystems and species have legal rights just like humans. This puts nature as a living entity at equal legal footing with humans, not as their property, such as Panama's Rights of Nature Law adopted in 2023.
Corporations harming these rights would be violating law. Such perspectives and laws can better support conservation and biodiversity protection, but inclusive implementation with women, youth, and indigenous communities is important here.
Aligning actions around the Rio Conventions
Integrating climate action and biodiversity action without duplicating mandates is fundamental if we are to address all three Rio Conventions -- climate change, desertification, and biodiversity.There was no structured discourse on Rio synergy in the conference.
There were talks about carbon trading and how local communities can participate and benefit from carbon trading marketplaces. If their ownership, stake, and decision-making remain, they can manage natural resources best without overexploitation. It will allow countries to maintain the carbon credit trade and reduce emissions sustainably.
For Bangladesh to make use of this market, mangrove restoration and wetland conservation are great areas to start.
The use of technology and AI in developing biodiversity information systems was met with optimism. Armenia and Colombia jointly committed to finance endangered species conservation through private sector engagement. There is hope to achieve all 23 targets by 2030, but things still do not look too good.
From a Global South perspective, we raised concerns about how biodiversity conservation should complement livelihoods, respect community experiences, and engage people of faith.
We must consider the Rio synergies, and we must ensure multi-stakeholder governance and multilateral cooperation. We urged governments and experts to create a structured method to measure impact on ecosystem recovery, species conservation status, livelihood resilience outcomes, and equitable benefit sharing.
Science should be able to influence policy-making and economics and create tripartite solutions. We have committed to nature, to the world, and to the people with the KMGBF. Without its implementation, we are failing ourselves.
Will the global review lead to stronger, measurable action before 2030? Will biodiversity finance and governance genuinely empower local communities?
The world does not need another declaration of concern about biodiversity loss. While we saw great progress in technical aspects, the success of that progress truly depends on political consensus.
If governments together can adopt these technical perspectives and put them into proper funding pathways, policy, and practice, there is hope for the future of biodiversity.
Kazi Amdadul Hoque is the Senior Director, Strategic Planning & Head of Climate Action at Friendship.

item.title: SAFF Championship: Pakistan cruise past Maldives 3-0, close in on semi-final spot. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan revived their semi-final hopes in the SAFF Championship with a commanding 3-0 victory over Maldives in their second Group B fixture at the National Football Stadium in Dhaka on Sunday.

A first-half brace from Najeebullah Bettani, alongside an early penalty converted by McKeal Aroon Abdullah, helped Pakistan register their first victory of the tournament and put themselves in a strong position to qualify for the last four.

Pakistan made an aggressive start and took the lead in the fourth minute when they were awarded a penalty.

McKeal Abdullah stepped up and calmly converted from the spot to give the Green Shirts an early advantage.

Pakistan continued to press forward and doubled their lead through Najeebullah, who produced a well-timed finish after Junaid Shah delivered an excellent cross from the left.

Najeebullah made a perfectly timed run into the box, got ahead of his marker and poked the ball home.

The forward then completed his brace with a superb individual effort. With Pakistan defending deep in their own half, the ball was cleared upfield, where Najeebullah brought it under control on the right before unleashing a powerful strike past the helpless Maldives goalkeeper.

Pakistan’s three-goal advantage at half-time reflected their attacking efficiency, with the side making the most of their opportunities to put the contest beyond their opponents.

Despite enjoying slightly more possession, Maldives struggled to translate it into meaningful attacking opportunities.

Pakistan, meanwhile, were more threatening in front of goal, registering 15 shots, including five on target, compared to Maldives’ seven attempts, only one of which tested the goalkeeper.

Both sides pushed for more goals after the interval, but neither could find the breakthrough as the second half ended goalless, leaving Pakistan with a convincing 3-0 victory.

The result marked a significant response from Pakistan following their 3-2 defeat against arch-rivals India in their opening Group B encounter on November 5.

Pakistan had trailed 3-0 at half-time in that match before producing a spirited late comeback.

Najeebullah and Alamgir Ghazi scored in stoppage time to reduce the deficit, but India held on to secure all three points.

The 2026 SAFF Championship, running from Nov 5 to 17 in Bangladesh, features six participating teams divided into two groups. Group ‘B’ comprises Pakistan, India and Maldives, while hosts Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan are in Group ‘A’.

The top two teams from each group will advance to the semi-finals.

With their victory over Maldives, Pakistan have moved into a stronger position in the qualification race but must now wait for the outcome of the remaining Group ‘B’ fixture between India and Maldives, scheduled for Nov 11.

Maldives will need a substantial victory over India to overtake Pakistan in the group standings and secure qualification.

Otherwise, Pakistan and India will progress to the semi-finals.

For Pakistan, the emphatic win provides a timely boost after their opening defeat and puts them within touching distance of a place in the last four.
